content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is the edible flower head of Brassica oleracea var. italica, native to the Mediterranean region. Fresh broccoli cooked with a small amount of vegetable oil retains a crisp texture and bright green color while enhancing the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the same family as cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, and kale.
Glucoraphanin levels increase during heat treatment, especially when sautéed in oil.
China and India are the world’s largest producers of broccoli.
Broccoli is often called “little trees” because its florets resemble tiny trees.
There are over 100 broccoli varieties differing in shape, color, and flavor.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One serving provides more than 100 % of the daily value for vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains beneficial phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have anti‑inflammatory and potential anticancer properties.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can cause bloating and gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables, including broccoli.

items.title: Possible nitrate buildup
items.content: Improper storage can increase nitrate levels; it is best to use fresh produce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oil‑cooked broccoli can be served as a side dish, added to stir‑fries, salads, pasta, or soups. For optimal vitamin A and K absorption, sauté over medium heat for 3‑5 minutes, avoiding overcooking to keep it crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh broccoli in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a small amount of moisture for up to 5 days. Cooked broccoli should be consumed within 2‑3 days, kept in an airtight container in the fridge.

pizza-with-meat-and-vegetables-from-froz.title: Pizza with meat and vegetables, frozen, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: A thin‑crust frozen pizza topped with meat (beef, ham, sausage) and vegetables (tomato, bell pepper, onion) – a convenient quick‑dinner option. The crust becomes crisp when baked, while the topping is aromatic and well‑balanced.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The thin crust is made from high‑grade flour, giving it a crunchy texture after baking.
The meat blend usually combines beef and pork for a rich flavor profile.
Vegetables are pre‑sautéed to retain bright color and aroma.
The pizza is stored frozen at -18 °C, preserving nutrients for up to 12 months.
Fast‑bake technology allows the pizza to be ready in 8‑12 minutes in a standard home oven.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply B1, B2, B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The pizza contains iron, zinc and magnesium, important for immunity and nerve function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables add fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Unlike sweet snacks, this pizza contains minimal simple sugars.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Salt used in the sauce and meat can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Meat ingredients may increase saturated fat intake, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The crust contains wheat, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats in some sauces
items.content: Some manufacturers use partially hydrogenated oils; check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Preheat the oven to 200 °C and bake the pizza for 8‑12 minutes until the crust is golden. Serve hot, optionally garnish with fresh basil or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen pizza in a freezer at -18 °C or lower. After thawing (no more than 2 hours at room temperature) cook immediately. Do not store thawed pizza for more than 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Tamale is a traditional dish made from corn masa (dough) with a filling, wrapped in corn husks or banana leaves and steamed. The NFS (No Fillings Specified) version is a plain masa without any added ingredients, intended as a versatile base for culinary use.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales have ancient roots in Mesoamerican cuisine and were used in ritual contexts.
They are traditionally prepared in large batches for holidays and family gatherings.
Corn masa in tamales is rich in carbohydrates and easily digestible.
Across the world there are hundreds of filling variations: meat, cheese, beans, vegetables, fruits.
Tamales can be made sweet or savory depending on the filling and seasoning.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Corn masa provides sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Corn flour contains fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The plain NFS version contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tamales supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn flour is naturally gluten‑free, safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Improper storage of cooked tamales can lead to bacterial growth, so follow proper refrigeration guidelines.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn‑based foods can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamale NFS can be boiled, steamed, or baked, then used as a base: add meat or vegetable fillings, serve with sauces, or incorporate into soups and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry tamale portions in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked tamales should be kept in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days or frozen for up to 2 months.
